cards.title: Sublinear-in-q prophet inequalities for q-matroid intersection
cards.formal: Is there a function \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to[1,\infty)\) with \(\lim_{q\to\infty}g(q)/q=0\) such that, for every sequence of independent nonnegative random values and every feasibility constraint given by the intersection of \(q\) matroids, some online irrevocable selection strategy obtains expected reward at least \(1/g(q)\) times the expected offline optimum? The arrival order is fixed in advance, all value distributions and constraints are known to the strategy, and the guarantee is independent of the number of elements.

source_formulation.text: Are there asymptotically better algorithms for the matroid intersection prophet inequality?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 17

cards.why: A prophet knows all random values before choosing a feasible set, while an online selector must commit before later values arrive. Matroid intersections capture many simultaneous resource constraints. Determining whether the approximation loss can grow sublinearly in their number would distinguish a limitation imposed by lack of future information from the performance of existing selection guarantees.
cards.status_note: The 2023 source leaves the general asymptotic improvement open, and the author’s June 2024 note retains a corresponding restricted stochastic-matching question. The checked lower bound is sublinear and does not refute the target. Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution; this is not an exhaustive guarantee of current openness.

progress.text: As checked against the 2023 source’s explicit correction, Kleinberg and Weinberg provide a linear-in-\(q\) upper guarantee and a square-root lower-bound construction; their originally claimed matching linear lower bound was erroneous.

importance.reason: This asks whether intersecting many independent feasibility constraints forces an essentially linear loss from sequential decisions even with full distributional knowledge and unlimited computation. Closing the gap would clarify a basic limitation of prophet inequalities and their use in stochastic allocation and mechanism design.

sentences: Independent random element values arrive one at a time in a fixed known order.
The selector must irrevocably choose a set that is independent in each of q given matroids.
It knows the value distributions, while the offline comparator sees all realized values before making its choice.
The question asks whether the ratio of their expected rewards can always be bounded by a function growing sublinearly in q.
The checked source improves a square-root lower obstruction but corrects an earlier erroneous linear lower-bound claim and leaves the gap open.

cards.definitions: Fix integers \(q,n\ge1\). The ground set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with elements arriving in the known order \(1,\ldots,n\). For each \(j\in[q]\), a matroid independence family \(\mathcal I_j\subseteq2^{[n]}\) contains \(\varnothing\), is hereditary, and satisfies augmentation: whenever \(A,B\in\mathcal I_j\) and \(|A|<|B|\), some \(b\in B\setminus A\) has \(A\cup\{b\}\in\mathcal I_j\). The feasible sets are \(\mathcal I=\bigcap_{j=1}^q\mathcal I_j\); repetitions among the matroids are allowed. For each \(t\), let \(D_t\) be an arbitrary Borel probability distribution on \([0,\infty)\) with finite first moment, and draw \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) independently with laws \(D_1,\ldots,D_n\). The offline optimum is \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)=\max_{S\in\mathcal I}\sum_{t\in S}X_t\), after all values have been revealed. An online strategy knows \(q,n,\mathcal I_1,\ldots,\mathcal I_q,D_1,\ldots,D_n\) in advance. Upon seeing \(X_t\), it accepts or rejects element \(t\) irrevocably. Its decision is a measurable function of \(t\), the observed prefix \(X_1,\ldots,X_t\), previous decisions and an internal random seed \(U\) uniform on \([0,1]\) and independent of all \(X_t\). Deterministic strategies may ignore \(U\). Every accepted prefix must be feasible, for every value sequence and seed, and previously accepted elements cannot be removed. Let \(S_{\mathcal A}(X,U)\) be the final accepted set and \(\operatorname{ALG}_{\mathcal A}(X,U)=\sum_{t\in S_{\mathcal A}(X,U)}X_t\). No bound on computation, distribution access or preprocessing is imposed; this is the information-theoretic online model. Exact distributions are part of the mathematical instance, not an implicit finite encoding or a sampling oracle. The target quantifiers are \(\exists g\;\forall q\ge1\;\forall n\ge1\;\forall(\mathcal I_j)_{j=1}^q\;\forall(D_t)_{t=1}^n\;\exists\mathcal A\) such that \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{ALG}_{\mathcal A}]\ge\mathbb E[\operatorname{OPT}]/g(q)\). Expectations include both the independent values and the independent internal seed. The first-moment assumption makes both expectations finite. The inequality also applies when the offline expectation is zero. The limit requirement means that for every \(\eta>0\), some \(q_0\) satisfies \(g(q)\le\eta q\) for all \(q\ge q_0\). The fixed arrival order represents any adversarially chosen order known before the random values are drawn; the order cannot adapt to their realizations.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the existence statement for one function \(g=o(q)\), including a policy with the stated guarantee for every instance, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation over all permitted strategies. Improving the constant in a linear \(Cq\) guarantee is insufficient. An \(o(q)\) result only for partition matroids, identical distributions, random arrival order or a bounded number of elements does not prove the full positive statement. A super-square-root lower bound that is itself \(o(q)\) does not refute it. There is no additional polynomial-time requirement.

context_blocks.text: The 2023 source asks whether asymptotically better matroid-intersection prophet inequalities exist. This card selects the \(o(q)\) improvement asked by the imported title, using the source’s unrestricted online-strategy benchmark rather than adding a polynomial-time computation requirement.

The source’s Theorem 7 records a general upper bound \(e(q+1)\) on the ratio of expected offline reward to expected online reward, where \(e\) is the base of the natural logarithm. The ratio compares two expectations, not an expectation of a ratio or a pointwise competitive guarantee.

The paper proves a lower bound \(q^{1/2+\Omega(1/\log\log q)}\), already for intersections of partition matroids with identical Bernoulli values. This improves a square-root obstruction while leaving room between the proved lower bound and linear upper bounds.

Footnote 3 explicitly corrects an earlier claimed \(\Omega(q)\) lower bound in Kleinberg and Weinberg’s work: that construction yields an \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) obstruction. The correction does not invalidate their linear upper bound. Thus the earlier linear lower-bound claim cannot be used as a resolution of this question.

Velusamy’s June 2024 open-problem note again asks for an asymptotic improvement in online stochastic hypergraph matching with Bernoulli values, a partition-matroid subcase. That note supports the persistence of a restricted version and does not claim a general-matroid solution.

cards.title: Randomized competitive ratio of list update
cards.formal: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio of online list update against an oblivious adversary in the full-cost model: \[\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}=\inf\{r\in[1,\infty):r\text{ is achievable under the definition below}\}.\] Give its value to absolute error at most \(1/100\). The same competitive factor must work for lists of every finite size, with an additive constant allowed to depend on the size and initial order. No predictions or advice about future requests are supplied.
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge1\), the item set is \([n]\) and an initial list \(L_0\) is a permutation of these items. A request sequence \(\sigma=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\in[n]^T\) has arbitrary finite length \(T\ge0\), is fixed independently of all online randomness, and is revealed one request at a time. The online rule must finish serving \(x_t\) before learning \(x_{t+1}\); it is not told the remaining sequence or its length. Accessing an item in current position \(j\), counting from one, costs \(j\). After this access, that item may be moved any distance toward the front at zero cost. Each other exchange of adjacent items costs one. Paid exchanges may be performed between accesses, including before serving a revealed request, and every such exchange is charged. The free move changes only the accessed item’s position and preserves the relative order of all other items. Items are never inserted or deleted. The total cost is the sum of access costs and paid exchanges. The offline optimum \(\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)\) is the minimum cost of a legal schedule starting from the same \(L_0\), with advance knowledge of all of \(\sigma\), under exactly these access and exchange rules. A randomized online rule chooses each finite legal service action using only the revealed request prefix, its previous actions and its private random state. Abstract probability distributions over actions are permitted, with no bound on computational work or memory; all expectations must be well defined. Each request is served with finitely many exchanges on each realization. A real \(r\ge1\) is achievable if \[\forall n\ge1\ \forall L_0\ \exists A_{n,L_0,r}\ \exists\beta_{n,L_0,r}\in[0,\infty)\ \forall T\ge0\ \forall\sigma\in[n]^T:\quad \mathbb E[\mathrm{cost}_{A_{n,L_0,r}}(\sigma)]\le r\,\mathrm{OPT}_{n,L_0}(\sigma)+\beta_{n,L_0,r}.\] The rule and finite additive constant are chosen before the future requests, so neither may depend on \(\sigma\) or \(T\). Expectation is over the algorithm’s randomness alone. The infimum is over such common factors \(r\); it need not be attained. This is the full-cost convention \(j\), not the partial-cost convention \(j-1\). All costs and the ratio are dimensionless.
cards.why: List update is a basic model of a data structure adapting to changing demand without knowing future accesses. Its optimal randomized ratio would quantify the value of randomization in a simple online problem whose deterministic analogue is well understood. The unresolved constant gap makes it a precise long-standing benchmark in competitive analysis.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 primary source states the classical randomized bounds \(1.5\le\rho_{\mathrm{LU}}\le1.6\) and defines access cost by the position counted from one. This interval has width \(0.1\), so it does not certify the required absolute error \(0.01\).

The same paper investigates algorithms assisted by predictions. Their guarantees involve additional information unavailable in the ordinary online problem specified here; those results do not settle the classical optimal ratio.

A related lower bound of \(1.50084\), proved by Ambühl, Gärtner and von Stengel, is explicitly for the partial-cost model, where the first item costs zero to access. Changing the charge by one on every request can change a competitive ratio, so that theorem is not asserted here as a stronger full-cost lower bound.

The additive constant is independent of the entire request sequence and its length. It permits a fixed initial-order cost but cannot absorb a cost that grows with the number of requests. The infimum formulation also permits a limiting optimal ratio without assuming that a best online rule exists.

cards.title: Adaptive regret in misspecified linear bandits
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and an integer \(p\ge0\) such that, for every \(d,k,T\in\mathbb N\) with \(d,T\ge1\) and \(k\ge d^2\), and every known feature matrix \(\Phi\in\mathbb R^{k\times d}\), there is one bandit policy \(\pi\) satisfying, simultaneously for every unknown mean-reward vector \(\mu\in\mathbb R^k\) with \(\max_i\mu_i-\min_i\mu_i\le1\), \[R_T(\pi,\mu)\le C[\log(2kdT)]^p\min\left\{T,\ d\sqrt T+\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)T\sqrt d,\ \frac{k}{d}\sqrt T\right\}?\] Here \(\varepsilon(\Phi,\mu)=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb R^d}\|\Phi\theta-\mu\|_\infty\). The policy may depend on \(\Phi,d,k,T\), but cannot be given \(\mu\), a fitting parameter \(\theta\), the misspecification level \(\varepsilon\), or an upper bound on that level. Use the Gaussian-noise model below.
cards.why: Features let a learner transfer information between arms, but approximation errors can make that transfer misleading. A policy that adapts to unknown error while preserving a controlled fallback would identify how much statistical benefit an imperfect model can safely provide. The requirement that one policy meet the bound at every error level is central: independently choosing a policy after learning the true error would answer a different question.
cards.status_note: Current openness is uncertain. The precise bound is speculative in the 2020 book; checked later primary results establish important related adaptation guarantees, but this review has not verified the full displayed simultaneous bound as a theorem or excluded its coverage by existing work. This card is individually formulated and retains that status limitation explicitly.

category_assignment.reason: The question asks for sequential prediction, exploration or regret guarantees under online feedback.

importance.reason: A substantial robustness and adaptation question for a foundational sequential-learning model. The simultaneous guarantee tests whether useful linear structure can be exploited without sacrificing controlled performance when that structure is inaccurate, across arbitrary known action geometries. Its importance is broader than optimizing a bound for one fixed action set.

sentences: The question asks for one bandit policy that adapts to unknown error in a linear reward model.
It must exploit accurate features while simultaneously obeying a uniform fallback bound when those features fit poorly.
The model has finitely many indexed arms, independent Gaussian observation noise and a known feature matrix of arbitrary geometry.
The displayed tradeoff comes from an explicit speculation in Bandit Algorithms, while later papers prove closely related partial guarantees.
The formulation is now precise, but the current openness of the complete simultaneous bound remains uncertain.

cards.definitions: There are \(k\) indexed arms, with \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\); row \(\Phi_i\) gives the known feature vector of arm \(i\). Different arms may have the same feature vector, and no full-rank assumption or bound on the entries of \(\Phi\) is imposed. The mean vector is fixed before play and does not change with time or the learner’s choices. In round \(t\in[T]\), the policy chooses \(A_t\in[k]\), then observes only \(Y_t=\mu_{A_t}+Z_t\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_T\) are independent standard real Gaussian random variables with mean zero and variance one, independent of the learner’s randomness. A policy for fixed known \((\Phi,d,k,T)\) is a collection of Borel-measurable maps from the history \(([k]\times\mathbb R)^{t-1}\) to the probability simplex \(\Delta_k=\{q\in[0,1]^k:\sum_iq_i=1\}\), one for each round; the selected arm is sampled from that distribution using fresh private randomness. These maps do not take the unknown environment as an argument. Thus the same policy must work for all allowed \(\mu\) for that fixed known instance. Expected regret is \(R_T(\pi,\mu)=\mathbb E_{\pi,\mu}[\sum_{t=1}^T(\max_{i\in[k]}\mu_i-\mu_{A_t})]\), with expectation over observation noise and policy randomness. It compares to the best fixed arm’s mean, not the largest realized noisy reward. For \(v\in\mathbb R^k\), \(\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|\). The infimum in the misspecification definition ranges over all real \(\theta\), with no norm constraint. The reward-range normalization bounds regret by \(T\); it does not bound the realized Gaussian observations. Logarithms in the displayed guarantee are natural. The single exponent \(p\) and multiplicative constant \(C\) are chosen before all instance parameters, so all hidden logarithmic losses are uniform powers of \(\log(2kdT)\). This is an information-theoretic policy-existence question: the number of reward observations is the resource, and no running-time, finite-precision representation or efficient implementation requirement is imposed on the measurable policies.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this policy-existence statement or its negation. A positive answer must provide the policy family and prove the simultaneous expected-regret bound with one universal \(C,p\), over the entire stated domain and without access to the misspecification level. A negative answer must rule out every universal pair \(C,p\), with an instance on which every policy has some admissible mean vector violating the bound; the violating mean vector may depend on the policy but is fixed before play. A guarantee only at zero misspecification, only for a known misspecification bound, or without the second uniform fallback term does not meet the target. No additive numerical tolerance applies to this asymptotic existence question.

context_blocks.text: The draft grouped two directions from the book. Section 24.4 makes the concrete conjectural claim with the minimum of \(d\sqrt T+\varepsilon T\sqrt d\) and \((k/d)\sqrt T\) when \(k\ge d^2\). This explicit simultaneous-adaptation statement is the card’s main target. Section 24.5 also asks more broadly for action-set-dependent regret characterizations; that broader direction is retained as context rather than silently folded into a second answer criterion.

The mathematical conventions are fixed against the chapter’s Gaussian model and the companion paper’s unit reward-range normalization. Indexed arms allow repeated feature rows, as in the book’s own lower-bound example. The present displayed bound also tracks every intermediate misspecification level; the two-case theorem alone is not recorded as a proof of that complete bound.

Hu, Yao, Zhang and Zhou’s July 2026 preprint uses misspecification-dependent guarantees for nonstationary bandits with changing feasible actions. Its principal claims concern dynamic regret and the variation of a time-dependent reward parameter. The checked statements do not directly assert the finite-action stationary bound on this card.

Current openness remains uncertain. The original book labels the displayed tradeoff speculative, and later work proves closely related adaptation results. This review recovers the exact target and checks several relevant theorem statements; it does not establish that no existing combination or later theorem already gives the complete guarantee.

cards.title: One forecaster with the optimal regret rate for every proper loss
cards.formal: For each fixed number \(K\ge 2\) of outcomes, does there exist one randomized online forecaster A, not given the loss function, such that for every bounded proper loss \(\ell\) its worst-case expected regret satisfies \(R_{A},\ell (T)\le C_{\ell},K\cdot (1+R*_{\ell},K(T))\cdot (\log (T+2))^{c_{\ell},K}\) for all \(T\ge 1\), for some constants \(C_{\ell},K>0\) and \(c_{\ell},K\ge 0\) independent of T? Here \(R*_{\ell},K\) is the minimax regret achievable by a forecaster tailored to that particular loss. This spells out the source’s “optimal up to constant or logarithmic factors in T” target; the additive one covers losses with zero or bounded optimal regret.
cards.why: Would establish whether a general-purpose probability forecaster can match every downstream user’s best possible learning rate without knowing that user’s loss. It refines universal sublinear regret into adaptation to the intrinsic difficulty of each scoring rule.
cards.status_note: Full forecasting model, proven simultaneous bounds and concluding question checked with the June arXiv record and subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No loss-universal minimax-rate result or impossibility was located. The displayed minimax comparison makes the asymptotic target explicit.

cards.definitions: The prediction space is the simplex \(\Delta _{K}=\{p\in \mathbb{R} ^{K}:p_{i}\ge 0,\sum p_{i}=1\}\). At round t, A chooses a possibly random \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\in \Delta _{K}\) from earlier revealed outcomes, then observes \(y_{t}\in \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\), where \(e_{i}\) is the ith unit vector. The adversary fixes \(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{T}\) in advance, knowing A but not its random bits. For a measurable loss \(\ell\):\(\Delta _{K}\times \{e_{1},\ldots ,e_{K}\}\to [- 1,1]\), propriety means \(E_{Y\sim p}\ell (p,Y)\le E_{Y\sim p}\ell (q,Y)\) for every \(p,q\in \Delta _{K}\); the minimizer need not be unique. Define \(Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)=E_{A}[\sum _{t=1}^{T} \ell (\mathrm{P}_{t},y_{t})]- \inf _{p\in \Delta _{K}}\sum _{t=1}^{T}\ell (p,y_{t})\). The expectation is over forecasting randomness, while the comparator is the best single fixed probability prediction in hindsight. Propriety makes the empirical outcome distribution a minimizing comparator. Set \(R_{A},\ell (T)=\sup _{y_{1}:T}Reg_{A},\ell (y_{1}:T)\), and \(R*_{\ell},K(T)=\inf _{B} R_{B},\ell (T)\), where B ranges over randomized online prediction strategies allowed to know \(\ell ,K\) and T. The desired A may know K and the horizon T, but its predictions are independent of which downstream loss is evaluated. Constants and logarithmic exponents may depend on the fixed loss and K; the asymptotic comparison is in T. This is an expected-regret comparison for each loss, not one simultaneous high-probability event over all losses. The question does not impose a particular polynomial running-time bound or a finite-precision implementation model; the target is the attainable online regret rate.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a loss-independent forecaster and prove the comparison for every bounded proper loss, or show that every such forecaster has some bounded proper loss for which its worst-case expected regret exceeds every allowed logarithmic-factor comparison with that loss’s minimax rate. Achieving \(\widetilde{O}\)\((\sqrt{T})\) for all losses alone does not settle the question, because some individual losses admit logarithmic or smaller regret.

context_blocks.title: Different users judge the same forecast differently
context_blocks.text: A probability forecast can be used by many downstream decision makers. Proper losses reward reporting the true probability distribution in expectation, but different losses penalize mistakes differently. The forecaster must issue the same \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\) before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

context_blocks.title: Worst-case optimal for a class can still be poor for an easy loss
context_blocks.text: For squared loss, logarithmic regret is attainable. A general guarantee of order \(\sqrt{T}\) can therefore be much worse than a user could obtain with a loss-specific forecaster. The target adapts to each loss’s own difficulty, rather than just the hardest loss in the class.

context_blocks.title: One predictor already adapts to an important subclass
context_blocks.text: The paper gives one efficient algorithm with \(\widetilde{O}\)\((K^{5/4}\sqrt{T})\) regret for every bounded proper loss and \(O(\beta  \log  T+\beta \sqrt{K} \log  K)\) for bounded \(\beta\)-smooth proper losses. It also extends logarithmic guarantees to a broader relative-smoothness class. These are substantial simultaneous guarantees, but do not characterize every individual proper loss.

context_blocks.title: The comparator cannot change its forecast each round
context_blocks.text: The hindsight benchmark is one fixed probability vector p, chosen after all outcomes are known. Competing with a different optimal \(p_{t}\) on every round would be a much stronger and generally impossible target under arbitrary outcome sequences.

context_blocks.title: No common random event is being asserted
context_blocks.text: For each fixed loss, average regret over A’s own randomization must have the required rate against every fixed outcome sequence. The statement does not claim that a single realized random trajectory satisfies all loss bounds with high probability.

The forecaster must issue the same \(\mathrm{P}_{t}\) before knowing which user’s loss will be used.

For squared loss, logarithmic regret is attainable. A general guarantee of order \(\sqrt{T}\) can therefore be much worse than a user could obtain with a loss-specific forecaster. The target adapts to each loss’s own difficulty, rather than just the hardest loss in the class.

The hindsight benchmark is one fixed probability vector p, chosen after all outcomes are known. Competing with a different optimal \(p_{t}\) on every round would be a much stronger and generally impossible target under arbitrary outcome sequences.
